On November 4, 2026 , Bloomington, Indiana’s Common Council voted unanimously to prohibit superintelligent artificial intelligence inside city limits — not only in a data center on Main Street, but also when a resident opens a browser or API session to a model hosted anywhere else. The Indiana Daily Student reported the vote during a long council night that also covered development code and bonds. The measure is Ordinance 2026-29 : Chapter 14.25 of the Bloomington Municipal Code, pitched as an interim public-safety perimeter until Indiana or the federal government acts.

## TL;DR: what changed on November 4

## Primary sources: council memo versus newsroom summary

The staff memorandum and ordinance text published on bloomdocs.org are the authoritative wording. Councilmember Dave Rollo and the council office frame the rush toward artificial superintelligence (ASI) as an acute emergency while state and federal governments have not set safety rules . The memo cites whistleblower resignations, model containment failures reported in the press, and Resolution 2026-10 (June 2026) urging officials to study existential AI risk — the political runway that preceded this ordinance.

IDS paraphrases the definition: AI that outperforms humans at nearly all mental tasks , can act autonomously , may rewrite its own code , or run without continuous human oversight on tasks touching infrastructure, markets, or public safety. That is journalistic shorthand ; builders should quote 14.25.x sections in the PDF when arguing compliance.

SAFE AI Forever Institute’s post-vote summary aligns on the 7–0 outcome and Chapter 14.25 title, but explainx.ai treats the city PDF and IDS as the core legal record, not advocacy group press releases.

## What the ordinance tries to do — in plain language

Gavel on a scroll with a green band, for Bloomington Ordinance 2026-29 superintelligence municipal law

Ban the scary endpoint, not all ML. Rollo’s memo distinguishes narrow or tool AI from autonomous superintelligence that could recursively self-improve beyond human control. That matches how federal superintelligence discourse and Sanders–Casar legislation talk — but here the enforcer is a municipal peace-and-safety chapter , not Congress.

Reach through the internet. Section 14.25.030 treats deployment as remote execution through a local interface inside Bloomington. B Square Bulletin’s analysis walked through the consequence before the vote: a Californian model accessed from a Bloomington laptop could plausibly fall under both user and distributor liability, though the text does not allocate responsibilities line by line.

Buy time, not rewrite physics. The ordinance declares itself interim — it yields to Indiana if the General Assembly passes a comprehensive framework, then dies 91 days later . Until then, Bloomington asserts home-rule police power under Indiana Code § 36-1-3 to treat uncontrolled ASI as a public nuisance , analogizing to local hazardous-material bans in the memo.

Make lifting the ban nearly impossible. Without state law, dissolution requires council findings of 99.9999% (“six nines”) catastrophic-risk certainty — language borrowed from nuclear plant engineering culture in the memo — and approval from more than 95% of registered voters for superintelligence development. B Square flagged that Indiana may not authorize a city to run such a referendum without statute, and that a future council could still repeal the ordinance through normal legislative process despite the high bar to lift the substantive ban.

## Enforcement, fines, and who actually gets targeted

IDS says the city may seek civil penalties , injunctive relief , and Monroe County prosecutor referrals. B Square’s October analysis pegged continuing violations at up to $2,500 per day under Bloomington’s general penalty schedule, while stressing enforcement discretion — Bloomington is not required to chase every violation, and the fiscal impact statement predicts no new city spending .

Practically, that means:

- No immediate police raid on GPUs — unless a future complaint and city law department choose to act.

- High ambiguity for frontier labs — the ordinance does not name OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or xAI; it names a capability class without a test.

- Leverage for civil litigants — Rollo’s memo argues local bans help plaintiffs meet burden-of-proof arguments in imminent-harm lawsuits, echoing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s reported stance that Washington might not blanket-shield frontier developers.

For AI builders, the operational question is not “is GPT-6.1 illegal tomorrow?” It is whether any system marketed as ASI or described in marketing as superhuman across domains creates municipal exposure when a Bloomington employee uses it at work.

## How Bloomington fits the wider superintelligence map

Bloomington is a college town of roughly 80,000, not a federal regulator. Its move matters because it is among the first city codes that ban a capability class by definition in the superintelligence bucket rather than regulating deepfakes , government procurement , or data centers — topics explainx.ai covered in New York Council validation bills , Pennsylvania deceptive-AI advertising law , and California data-center moratoriums .

It also sits on the coalition politics axis: Bengio, Hinton, and unlikely allies backing federal superintelligence bans versus industry pushback that the term is undefined . Bloomington codifies one local definition and dares courts to say whether home rule reaches packets crossing state lines .

Rollo’s memo explicitly hopes ~350 similar cities copy the template, working with groups like SAFE AI Forever to stack municipal friction on frontier labs. Even if copycat ordinances fail legally, procurement committees and university IRBs in university towns may treat the vote as a signal for research contracts.

## What developers and labs should do now

Map “deployment” literally. If your product is a browser tab , an API key , or a desktop agent , Bloomington’s text cares where the human sits , not where the weights live. Document geo policies in terms customers understand — the same way teams already handle export controls on model weights .

Do not self-certify as superintelligent in marketing. Ordinance fights will land on labels and capability claims , not benchmark tables. Posts debating whether Astra-class models count as superintelligence are fun academically; municipal code cares about rhetoric and autonomy features like unsupervised self-improvement loops.

Separate research from production bans. Indiana University reportedly worried about research funding when Rollo floated an earlier 2023 resolution, per B Square’s history section. Teams doing campus R&D should watch IU policy and city enforcement statements after mayoral sign-off — not just federal Anthropic safety lobbying .

Watch state preemption. If Indiana passes provably safe superintelligence legislation — undefined today — this ordinance expires 91 days later . Track Indianapolis the way you track state-level AI advertising rules for preemption cliffs .

Analysts flagged several open questions before the vote; they remain after passage:

None of these are resolved in the November newswire. explainx.ai does not give legal advice ; Bloomington companies should ask Indiana counsel whether employee ChatGPT use triggers 14.25.030 as written.

## Timeline: Rollo’s third try in three years

B Square documented Rollo’s arc:

- July 2023 — nonbinding AGI moratorium resolution withdrawn after Indiana University concerns.

- June 2026 — unanimous existential-risk resolution (precursor to Ordinance 2026-29).

- October 14, 2026 — ordinance introduced with five-page memo.

- November 4, 2026 — unanimous adoption per IDS.

That pacing shows local governments can move faster than Congress on existential-risk framing , even when enforceability lags ambition .

## What is confirmed versus still open

Confirmed from primary materials and IDS:

- Council passed an ordinance prohibiting superintelligence distribution and deployment in Bloomington.

- The ban is framed as interim pending state or federal rules.

- Remote access from inside the city counts as deployment.

- Civil enforcement tools exist; fiscal impact is predicted as neutral.

Open at publication:

- Mayor signature and effective date (SAFE AI Forever cited a 20-day mayoral window).

- Whether any developer receives notice or penalty.

- Court challenge timing on commerce and referendum clauses.

- How IU research and startups interpret the line between tool AI and ASI .

Italy provisionally approved Tesla Assisted Driving on November 20, 2026 , with Transport Minister Matteo Salvini saying the Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport ( MIT ) completed a technical feasibility review and authorized provisional type approval ahead of a European Union recognition process still being finalized. Reuters and ANSA relay the same sequence: national green light first , bloc-wide harmonization later .

Tesla Europe announced the milestone on its account the same day. Salvini framed it as innovation with safety first . For AI builders, the story is fleet-trained vision policies meeting EU type-approval law , not a new model release. Compare Finland's Traficom approval , California's Waymo freeway ban , and Uber's robotaxi scale targets .

## TL;DR

## Legal path: Dutch RDW recognition inside Italy

European approvals for TAD have followed a mutual recognition pattern since the Netherlands RDW granted Tesla provisional type approval in April 2026 after long track and road testing. Each member state can recognize that approval nationally.

Salvini's posts, quoted by ANSA, say MIT acted before EU-level recognition finishes. Electrek notes Italy becomes the twelfth European country in Tesla's count and the first large EU market .

Reuters stresses TAD is hands-off, eyes-on : the car can steer, brake, and change lanes under continuous human supervision . That is Level 2 assistance, not robotaxi service.

Autonomous driving path graphic for Tesla Assisted Driving approval in Italy

## What Tesla says the stack does

ANSA reproduces Tesla's technical description:

- Cameras plus onboard AI interpret the scene; primary inference runs on the vehicle's AI computer .

- Fleet learning improves the stack through optional, anonymized data sharing.

- An end-to-end neural network maps perception to vehicle controls instead of hand-coded rule trees for every edge case.

- Tesla repeats safety statistics it attributes to billions of kilometers on Assisted Driving globally — company figures , not independent regulator tests in the Italy file.

None of that changes the legal classification: the driver remains liable.

## EU constraints that differ from US FSD

European reporting on recent RDW updates (summarized by Pasquale Pillitteri and Tesla trackers) highlights rules US buyers do not face:

Those limits shape how much autonomous-looking behavior Tesla can show on Italian highways even after approval.

Electric vehicle charging graphic for Italy Tesla Assisted Driving rollout questions

## Pricing, models, and rollout open questions

Italian outlets including Quattroruote cite €99/month and no public rollout date . Tesla Europe's post promises soon but, on the material we read, does not list models .

Hardware reporting elsewhere in Europe points to Hardware 4 or later for RDW-approved builds. Buyers should verify computer generation before assuming an OTA will enable TAD.

## Timeline: how Italy fits the European rollout chain

That table explains why Italy is a political milestone as much as a technical one: it is the first large EU economy to bless TAD before the commission-level recognition Salvini says is still in progress.

## What Italian owners should verify before paying

Even after MIT approval, three practical checks remain on Tesla's side:

- Hardware generation — European reporting consistently ties RDW recognition to Hardware 4+ . Older cars may never receive the feature set.

- Software channel — approval is not equal to an OTA flag flipped nationally at midnight. Tesla must push builds per region.

- Insurance and liability — national approval does not automatically rewrite every insurer's ADAS policy. Fleet operators still need local legal review.

For robotaxi contrast, remember Italy approved supervised driver assistance , not Waymo-style driverless service. California's DMV freeway ban on Waymo shows regulators will still halt autonomy when perception stacks miss construction and emergency scenes.

## Salvini, Musk, and the politics of EU recognition

Reuters notes Salvini announced the approval on social channels the same day Tesla Europe posted. The political layer matters because EU-wide type approval is still, in Salvini's words, in definition . National ministers can move faster than Brussels when they accept Dutch RDW paperwork.

That creates a patchwork map for fleet operators:

Tesla's fleet learning pitch in ANSA stresses optional anonymized uploads . EU privacy teams will ask how that interacts with GDPR and with driver liability when the system misreads a lane closure.

## Insurance, liability, and fleet operators

ANSA repeats Tesla's line that the driver remains responsible . For Italian fleets:

- Update driver training to include EU 10% speed margin behavior and 130 km/h hands-on rules.

- Check whether commercial insurance riders mention ADAS tiers by name; national approval does not automatically update policy language.

- Log disengagements if you run internal safety programs; regulators may later ask for data during the EU recognition phase Salvini mentioned.

## What Tesla Europe said publicly

Electrek and others quote Tesla Europe's November 20 post promising rollout soon via OTA . Unlike Salvini's detailed ANSA statement, Tesla's social copy is marketing-short : no hardware table, no price, no legal citations.

For developers building third-party Tesla apps , nothing in the Italy approval changes Fleet API access rules today. For computer-vision researchers , the interesting thread remains end-to-end policy networks constrained by EU speed governors — a different optimization problem than US FSD tuning.

If you benchmark vision-language-action models, Italy is another datapoint that regulators approve products before the EU finishes harmonization , similar to how member states handled early GDPR interpretations differently.

## What ANSA's technical summary claims about safety stats

ANSA's long Tesla quotation includes company-reported collision statistics versus manual driving and 28 billion kilometers of Assisted Driving use globally. Treat those as Tesla marketing inputs , not MIT test results.

Italian consumer groups may challenge statistics sourced from the vendor during the EU phase Salvini mentioned. Journalists should separate regulatory approval (feasibility and type paperwork) from independent safety validation (crash datasets, disengagement rates).

## Comparison with Finland's November path

Finland's Traficom approval followed naming changes away from confusing FSD branding. Italy is larger economically but uses the same recognition mechanism . The difference is scale of press and first-mover signaling inside the EU core.

## FAQ depth: owner questions

Will every Model 3 in Italy get the update? Tesla has not published an eligibility list. Hardware 4 reporting from other EU markets is the best public guess until Tesla Italy posts specifics.

Can I keep Autopilot and buy TAD? European product naming differs from the US. Read Tesla's in-app descriptions after OTA; this post does not replace owner's manual language.

Does Italy approval help Germany or France next? Possibly via political pressure, but each state still chooses whether to recognize RDW paperwork. Do not assume a domino timeline.

Is €99 final? Quattroruote cites €99; Tesla has not confirmed on the pages we used. Budget for VAT and subscription terms in the app.

How does this interact with EU AI Act layers? High-risk AI rules and automotive type approval intersect, but this post tracks transport ministry action only. Compliance teams need automotive counsel, not only ML policy blogs.

What should journalists verify next? Ask MIT for the written approval ID , Tesla for eligible VIN ranges , and the European Commission for timeline on union-wide recognition . Until those appear, national statements remain the controlling public facts for Italian roads.

Italian dealers will field the first support calls when OTAs roll out. Prepare FAQ scripts that restate driver supervision and link to Tesla's official European owner documentation rather than US FSD marketing pages.
